atoms.text:
In Jamaica, 1831, the cane harvest runs through Christmas. I think of my grandmother, who was brought here as a girl and renamed Anne; her Akan name survives only in her faded memories, I have never learned it. We cut cane from first light, hands raw from the leaves. The mill does not stop. Last week, a man from the next estate was flogged for slowing his pace.
They say the preacher, Samuel Sharpe, is calling for a strike. At night, we whisper about the rebellion spreading across the island. We talk of fires in the fields, plantations burning. I am sure that it will reach us, I feel ready for it. For the first time, the overseer listens for us as much as we listen for him.

atoms.text:
In the Niger Delta, 1897, news travels fast after the British massacred our people and burned Benin City. The Oba (King) was captured and the British took over control. Traders like me feel the change immediately. The Royal Niger Company sets new prices for palm oil and demands taxes. I carry the seeds downriver with a pass stamped in English. Without it, soldiers could seize my goods.
Missionaries have opened a school nearby. My son now writes letters for others, in a language that brings him closer to power but further from our elders' ways. Authority no longer sits where it used to. It arrives by steamer, is backed by guns, and leaves little space for refusal.

b: ++Benin City was burned and many people were massacred by the British in 1897.
The Oba remained in power during British colonialsm.
The trade was independent from British influence.
++Nigerian traders have to adhere to prices set by the Royal Niger Company.
++Missionary schools teach colonised children the English language.

atoms.text:
I arrived in Birmingham in 1964, some years after the Indian Partition drove my family from Amritsar to Lahore. I thought I knew Britain from my schoolbooks, the reality however, was a run down boarding house and shops with signs in the window: “No coloureds.”
I found work in a foundry through another Pakistani man. The hours are long, the pay just enough to send money home. In our free time, we gather in our cramped flat and listen to music and news on the radio. The buses are full of faces that turn away, but in our small rooms, speaking Urdu and Punjabi, we rebuild something familiar. I came because of my family. My sister writes me that my niece will be able to afford her school fee thanks to the money I send her.

b: ++The Partition led to the narrator and his family fleeing to Lahore.
++Hamza lives together with several other migrant workers from Pakistan.
++The narrator sends money to his family in Pakistan.
His daughter goes to school in Birmingham.
